subject: ELA
title: START HERE · Goodall study guide · Grade 6
teach: A memoir tells about real events in the writer’s life. Read Goodall’s whole memoir first so you understand what happened.
On your second reading, ask: What problems did she face? What did she learn? How did her work change over time?
When a question names a paragraph, reread that paragraph and the sentences around it. Use a detail from that part to explain your answer.
The topic is what a text is about. This memoir is about Jane Goodall’s work with chimpanzees. The main idea tells the most important point about that topic.
Goodall keeps trying, watches carefully, gains the chimps’ trust, and makes discoveries. Help from other people also supports her work.
A good main idea fits the whole memoir. Check it against the beginning, middle, and ending. One exciting event is a detail, not the main idea of the whole text.
Read the sentence around an unfamiliar word. Try a meaning, put it into the sentence, and check whether it makes sense.
Vanished means disappeared. “The deer vanished into the bushes” means the deer could no longer be seen.
Miserable means very unhappy or uncomfortable. “The cold rain made the wait miserable” shows discomfort.
Irritable means easily annoyed. An irritable person may get upset over a small interruption.
Threateningly means in a way that warns of possible harm. A dog that growls threateningly may be warning someone to stay back.
Impetuous means acting quickly without thinking enough. Cutting fabric before measuring it can be an impetuous choice.
Dominate means to control or have power over. Someone who interrupts everyone may try to dominate a discussion.

A subject tells who or what a clause is about. A verb tells an action or a state of being. A clause has a subject and a verb. An independent clause is a complete thought: “Maya kept notes.” A dependent clause needs more to finish its meaning: “Although the camera failed.”
Use a comma before and, but, or so when the word joins two complete thoughts: “The camera failed, but Maya kept notes.” Each side can stand alone.
Do not add a comma just because you see and. “Maya checked the camera and changed the battery” has one subject doing two actions.
Use a comma after a dependent clause at the beginning: “Although the camera failed, Maya kept notes.” The comma goes where the opening clause ends.
Use a comma after a long opening phrase: “After several hours beside the marsh, Maya packed her notebook.” This opening is a phrase because it does not have its own subject and verb.
Use a comma after an opening transition: “For example, Maya recorded the time.” Other examples are “In fact,” and “After all,”.
Use commas in a list of three or more things: “She packed paper, pencils, and binoculars.” In these questions, include the comma before the final and. This is called a serial comma.
The author’s purpose is the reason the author wrote the text. Ask: What does Goodall want readers to learn or understand?
Goodall informs readers about her research and what she learned about chimps. She tells about her own experiences and explains why the discoveries mattered.
Her feelings make the memoir interesting, but entertainment is not her only purpose. Her observations also teach readers about chimpanzees.
Goodall learned that chimps use tools and can change materials to make tools. David stripped leaves from a twig before using it to get termites.
She learned that chimps are individuals. They have different personalities, and their family relationships affect how they act.
She also saw young chimps learning from others. Chimps use calls and gestures to share information. Some gestures look like human gestures, but their calls are not the same as human language.
When you explain a discovery, tell what she saw and what it helped her understand. Do not make a bigger claim than the detail supports.
A personality trait describes how a person usually thinks or acts. Choose a trait, name an action from the text, and explain how the action shows that trait.
Goodall is persistent: she keeps trying after setbacks. She is patient: she gives the chimps time to get used to her. She is careful: she writes down details from her observations.
Her success came from these choices and from help from other people. Success does not mean she was never afraid or that she did everything alone.
A memoir is nonfiction about real experiences from the writer’s own life. The writer looks back and explains what those experiences meant.
Goodall took part in the events she describes. She uses first-person words such as I and my, tells what happened, and shares her thoughts and feelings.
The word I alone does not prove that a text is a memoir. A made-up story can use I, too. A memoir tells real personal experiences and reflects on them.
A memoir usually focuses on a meaningful part of a person’s life. An autobiography usually covers more of the person’s life.

model.prompt: Original parallel scenario: In a real first-person account, Noor recalls months of failed garden measurements, explains how she changed her method and reflects on learning to trust checked evidence. Explain purpose, a trait and memoir features.
model.reasoning: Separate purpose from topic: she explains a learning process and its meaning, not simply “gardens.” Connect action to trait: repeated checking and revised measurements support careful persistence. Establish genre using real personal events, selected months and reflection; “I” alone would not prove memoir.
model.answer: Noor informs readers about developing reliable measurements and reflects on learning. Revising and checking evidence supports careful persistence. The real first-person experiences from a selected period, together with reflection, make this a memoir.

guided.prompt: Original scenario: After several afternoons beside the empty stage, Luis tested the microphone and recorded its volume. Which explanation is correct?
options: The opening phrase is set off; tested and recorded share Luis, so “and” needs no automatic comma.
“And” always separates two independent clauses.
The opening phrase contains its own subject and verb.
A comma must separate Luis from tested.
guided.rationale: “After several afternoons beside the empty stage” is an introductory phrase; Luis is the subject of both predicates.

practice.prompt: Which main idea connects Goodall’s early problems with the research center at the end?
options: Patient observation, persistence and support can produce discoveries and lasting research.
Every encounter made the chimps immediately trust her.
Research succeeds only when a person works without help.
The whole account explains only how to set up a camp.
practice.rationale: The idea spans difficulty, learning, collaboration and the later result.

repair.teach: The idea spans difficulty, learning, collaboration and the later result. Connect the early problem, the work and the later result.
repair.prompt: A real account begins with failed weather measurements and ends with a useful class forecast. Which idea spans both?
options: One early failure describes the whole project.
The final forecast makes the earlier work irrelevant.
Weather measurements never require checking.
Careful improvement can turn setbacks into useful knowledge.
repair.rationale: Connect the early problem, the work and the later result.

practice.prompt: Why did Goodall write this memoir?
options: To give a complete instruction manual for keeping wild chimps as pets.
To entertain only, without conveying research or explaining discoveries.
To invent an imaginary adventure whose events are presented as fiction.
To inform through remembered research experiences and reflect on what they revealed.
practice.rationale: Her first-person experiences communicate information and its personal and scientific meaning.

repair.teach: Her first-person experiences communicate information and its personal and scientific meaning. Facts and reflection can work together in a personal nonfiction account.
repair.prompt: An author recalls learning to repair bicycles and explains what mistakes taught her. What combined purpose fits?
options: To inform through personal experience and reflect on learning.
To provide only a list of bicycle brands.
To describe her whole life from birth.
To claim every remembered event is fiction.
repair.rationale: Facts and reflection can work together in a personal nonfiction account.

practice.prompt: In paragraph 39, Goodall explains why changing a twig into a tool was important. How does this help her inform readers?
options: It changes the account into a list of fictional inventions.
It proves that a description of actions never informs readers.
It gives readers instructions to approach and feed wild animals.
It helps readers understand the importance of the observation, beyond what happened.
practice.rationale: An explanation of importance informs and invites reflection.

repair.teach: An explanation of importance informs and invites reflection. Purpose is developed when an author explains importance as well as events.
repair.prompt: A memoir explains why a first successful hearing aid changed the author’s participation in class. What does explaining “why” contribute?
options: It helps readers understand the event’s importance.
It removes the connection to the author’s experience.
It makes every detail equally important.
It changes the writing into a fictional script.
repair.rationale: Purpose is developed when an author explains importance as well as events.

practice.prompt: In paragraphs 8–13, Goodall keeps trying and changes how she watches the chimps. Which personality trait does this show?
options: Persistence: she keeps working and changes her approach despite setbacks.
Carelessness: she never considers how her approach affects the chimps.
Impatience: she abandons observation as soon as it becomes difficult.
Fearlessness: the evidence proves she never feels afraid anywhere in the account.
practice.rationale: Continued effort plus adjustment supports persistence; it does not show an absolute absence of fear.

repair.teach: Continued effort plus adjustment supports persistence; it does not show an absolute absence of fear. Name a trait the actions actually support; avoid absolute claims.
repair.prompt: An observer waits several days and changes viewing positions after disturbing nesting birds. Which trait fits the actions?
options: Patient persistence supported by adjustment.
Certainty that every bird is identical.
Unwillingness to continue learning.
Total absence of fear in every circumstance.
repair.rationale: Name a trait the actions actually support; avoid absolute claims.

practice.prompt: What does adding details to her notes each evening in paragraph 46 show about Goodall?
options: She wants to replace observed events with more exciting invented ones.
She can remember every event perfectly without records.
She works carefully to preserve fresh observations for later research.
She believes notes are unnecessary once she has watched an animal.
practice.rationale: The timing and recordkeeping action support carefulness, without requiring a perfect-memory claim.

repair.teach: The timing and recordkeeping action support carefulness, without requiring a perfect-memory claim. Specific recordkeeping supports carefulness, not being perfect.
repair.prompt: A student dates sketches and checks notes immediately after an experiment. What trait has direct support?
options: A wish to invent missing results.
Carefulness in preserving evidence.
Disinterest in what occurred.
Perfect recall without any records.
repair.rationale: Specific recordkeeping supports carefulness, not being perfect.

practice.prompt: Which detail shows a chimp changing material to make a tool?
options: David uses grass, then strips leaves from a twig to make it useful for termite fishing.
Several chimps gather where fruit is available.
Goodall describes David’s hair and beard.
A chimp sits near a tree while rain falls.
practice.rationale: Changing the twig for a purpose adds evidence of making or changing a tool.

repair.teach: Changing the twig for a purpose adds evidence of making or changing a tool. Look for a purposeful change to material, not simply its presence.
repair.prompt: A crow bends a wire into a hook before using it to retrieve food. Which observation specifically supports tool change?
options: The food is inside a container.
The crow changes the wire’s shape for the task.
The crow stands beside the container.
A person watches the crow.
repair.rationale: Look for a purposeful change to material, not simply its presence.

practice.prompt: What did Goodall learn about chimp personalities and relationships in paragraphs 48–49 and54–56?
options: Chimp calls prove their language and human language are identical.
All chimps have the same temperament and respond identically.
Chimps show individual differences, family care and learned social behavior.
Young chimps never learn from other members of their family.
practice.rationale: Different named individuals and family learning support this bounded conclusion.

repair.teach: Different named individuals and family learning support this bounded conclusion. Separate the observed differences and care from unsupported universal claims.
repair.prompt: One young animal approaches new objects while another stays back; older animals groom a youngster. Which conclusion stays within this evidence?
options: No animal ever learns from others.
Every species has the same social rules.
All animals have identical responses.
Individuals differ, and the group shows care of a youngster.
repair.rationale: Separate the observed differences and care from unsupported universal claims.

practice.prompt: Which answer best explains why this text is a memoir?
options: It describes animals, so it belongs to a fictional animal story.
It records every event from birth to death in chronological order.
It uses “I,” so it must be nonfiction even if the events were invented.
It recounts real, selected personal experiences in first person and includes reflection.
practice.rationale: Memoir combines real personal experience, selected scope and reflection; a pronoun alone does not show genre.

repair.teach: Memoir combines real personal experience, selected scope and reflection; a pronoun alone does not show genre. Use truth claim, personal perspective, selected scope and reflection together.
repair.prompt: A writer recounts a real summer helping at a shelter and reflects on her changed view of adoption. Which genre explanation fits?
options: Memoir: selected real personal experiences with reflection.
Biography, because any text about a person is written by someone else.
A complete autobiography, because it covers every year of her life.
Fiction, because the writer reports feelings.
repair.rationale: Use truth claim, personal perspective, selected scope and reflection together.

practice.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a comma and a joining word between TWO complete thoughts?
options: The class compared observations, recording the results.
The class compared observations and recorded the results.
The class compared observations, and the teacher recorded the results.
Because the class compared observations, the teacher recorded the results.
practice.rationale: “The class compared observations” and “the teacher recorded the results” can each stand alone.

repair.teach: “The class compared observations” and “the teacher recorded the results” can each stand alone. Both “the gate was locked” and “the caretaker had a spare key” stand alone.
repair.prompt: Which sentence joins two independent clauses with comma plus “yet”?
options: The gate was locked, yet the caretaker had a spare key.
Although the gate was locked, the caretaker entered.
The caretaker checked the gate and unlocked it.
The gate was locked, blocking the entrance.
repair.rationale: Both “the gate was locked” and “the caretaker had a spare key” stand alone.

practice.prompt: Which sentence puts the comma after the opening dependent clause?
options: Although the trail, was muddy our group continued slowly.
Although, the trail was muddy our group continued slowly.
Although the trail was muddy, our group continued slowly.
Although the trail was muddy our group, continued slowly.
practice.rationale: The dependent clause ends after “muddy”; the comma marks the boundary before the independent clause.

repair.teach: The dependent clause ends after “muddy”; the comma marks the boundary before the independent clause. The introductory dependent clause is “If the bus arrives early.”
repair.prompt: Choose the correct boundary in “If the bus arrives early we can visit the library.”
options: If the bus arrives early we can, visit the library.
If, the bus arrives early we can visit the library.
If the bus arrives early, we can visit the library.
If the bus arrives, early we can visit the library.
repair.rationale: The introductory dependent clause is “If the bus arrives early.”

practice.prompt: Which list correctly uses commas, including a comma before the final and?
options: I packed a notebook, a pencil and, a ruler.
I packed, a notebook, a pencil and a ruler.
I packed a notebook a pencil, and a ruler.
I packed a notebook, a pencil, and a ruler.
practice.rationale: Commas divide the three items; the requested style also places one before the final “and.”

repair.teach: Commas divide the three items; the requested style also places one before the final “and.” Separate the three sewing items; do not place a comma after the verb.
repair.prompt: Using SERIAL-COMMA style, choose the correctly punctuated series.
options: We sorted buttons, ribbons and, zippers.
We sorted, buttons, ribbons and zippers.
We sorted buttons, ribbons, and zippers.
We sorted buttons ribbons, and zippers.
repair.rationale: Separate the three sewing items; do not place a comma after the verb.

practice.prompt: Which sentence uses a comma after a long opening phrase and does not add an extra comma between two actions?
options: After several hours, beside the pond Lena packed her bag, and returned home.
After several hours beside the pond, Lena packed her bag, and returned home.
After several hours beside the pond, Lena packed her bag and returned home.
After several hours beside the pond Lena packed, her bag and returned home.
practice.rationale: The introductory phrase ends after “pond.” Lena is the shared subject of “packed” and “returned.”

repair.teach: The introductory phrase ends after “pond.” Lena is the shared subject of “packed” and “returned.” The phrase ends at “station”; Jo is the shared subject of checked and bought.
repair.prompt: Choose the correctly punctuated long phrase plus compound predicate.
options: Near the entrance, of the crowded station Jo checked the timetable and bought a ticket.
Near the entrance of the crowded station Jo checked, the timetable and bought a ticket.
Near the entrance of the crowded station, Jo checked the timetable, and bought a ticket.
Near the entrance of the crowded station, Jo checked the timetable and bought a ticket.
repair.rationale: The phrase ends at “station”; Jo is the shared subject of checked and bought.

practice.prompt: Which sentence correctly puts a comma after the opening words “After all”?
options: After all the notebook preserves the observations.
After all the, notebook preserves the observations.
After, all the notebook preserves the observations.
After all, the notebook preserves the observations.
practice.rationale: The comma follows the complete introductory transition “After all.” The main clause is the notebook preserves the observations. Check the phrase’s function rather than inserting a comma after its first word.

repair.teach: An introductory transition such as “After all,” “In fact,” or “For example,” is normally set off from the sentence by a comma in the style used here. A transition explains the relationship between ideas. It is not automatically a dependent clause: look for a subject and verb before classifying the sentence.
repair.prompt: Fresh application: use a comma after the introductory transition “As a result.” Which version places it at that boundary?
options: As, a result the team changed its plan.
As a result, the team changed its plan.
As a result the, team changed its plan.
As a result the team changed its plan.
repair.rationale: Set off the introductory transition as a unit before the main clause. It has no subject–verb pair of its own and is not a dependent clause.

practice.prompt: In the memoir, the chimps vanished from view. What does “vanished” mean in this context?
options: disappeared
stayed visible
became louder
moved closer
practice.rationale: “vanished” means disappeared. Explain which action or condition in the sentence supports that meaning.

repair.teach: Use the surrounding action or condition: “vanished” means disappeared. Substitute the meaning and check whether it fits.
repair.prompt: In a new situation, which meaning of “vanished” should stay the same?
options: became louder
disappeared
stayed visible
moved closer
repair.rationale: The core meaning is disappeared; a new context changes the situation, not the word’s core meaning here.

practice.prompt: Cold rain made the long wait miserable. What does “miserable” mean in this context?
options: very unhappy or uncomfortable
well prepared
curious but cheerful
powerful and confident
practice.rationale: “miserable” means very unhappy or uncomfortable. Explain which action or condition in the sentence supports that meaning.

repair.teach: Use the surrounding action or condition: “miserable” means very unhappy or uncomfortable. Substitute the meaning and check whether it fits.
repair.prompt: In a new situation, which meaning of “miserable” should stay the same?
options: curious but cheerful
very unhappy or uncomfortable
well prepared
powerful and confident
repair.rationale: The core meaning is very unhappy or uncomfortable; a new context changes the situation, not the word’s core meaning here.

practice.prompt: Noise disturbed the irritable dog. What does “irritable” mean in this context?
options: easily annoyed
unable to move
eager to cooperate
hard to notice
practice.rationale: “irritable” means easily annoyed. Explain which action or condition in the sentence supports that meaning.

repair.teach: Use the surrounding action or condition: “irritable” means easily annoyed. Substitute the meaning and check whether it fits.
repair.prompt: In a new situation, which meaning of “irritable” should stay the same?
options: eager to cooperate
easily annoyed
unable to move
hard to notice
repair.rationale: The core meaning is easily annoyed; a new context changes the situation, not the word’s core meaning here.

practice.prompt: The dog bared its teeth threateningly. What does “threateningly” mean in this context?
options: in a way that signals possible harm
in a way that shows approval
without making a sound
with great accuracy
practice.rationale: “threateningly” means in a way that signals possible harm. Explain which action or condition in the sentence supports that meaning.

repair.teach: Use the surrounding action or condition: “threateningly” means in a way that signals possible harm. Substitute the meaning and check whether it fits.
repair.prompt: In a new situation, which meaning of “threateningly” should stay the same?
options: without making a sound
in a way that signals possible harm
in a way that shows approval
with great accuracy
repair.rationale: The core meaning is in a way that signals possible harm; a new context changes the situation, not the word’s core meaning here.

practice.prompt: The impetuous designer cut before measuring. What does “impetuous” mean in this context?
options: acting suddenly without enough thought
making a careful long-term plan
waiting for stronger evidence
speaking very quietly
practice.rationale: “impetuous” means acting suddenly without enough thought. Explain which action or condition in the sentence supports that meaning.

repair.teach: Use the surrounding action or condition: “impetuous” means acting suddenly without enough thought. Substitute the meaning and check whether it fits.
repair.prompt: In a new situation, which meaning of “impetuous” should stay the same?
options: waiting for stronger evidence
acting suddenly without enough thought
making a careful long-term plan
speaking very quietly
repair.rationale: The core meaning is acting suddenly without enough thought; a new context changes the situation, not the word’s core meaning here.

practice.prompt: One individual could dominate the group. What does “dominate” mean in this context?
options: control or have power over
imitate another exactly
avoid all contact with
measure the size of
practice.rationale: “dominate” means control or have power over. Explain which action or condition in the sentence supports that meaning.

repair.teach: Use the surrounding action or condition: “dominate” means control or have power over. Substitute the meaning and check whether it fits.
repair.prompt: In a new situation, which meaning of “dominate” should stay the same?
options: avoid all contact with
control or have power over
imitate another exactly
measure the size of
repair.rationale: The core meaning is control or have power over; a new context changes the situation, not the word’s core meaning here.

independentCheck.prompt: Goodall describes both her research and her feelings. Which answer best explains why?
options: She helps readers understand the research process and her personal experience of it.
She argues that every chimp responds to every person in the same way.
She presents feelings instead of any factual observations.
She writes a field-safety checklist for all readers to follow.
independentCheck.rationale: A memoir can inform while letting readers understand the narrator’s changing perspective.

repair.teach: A memoir can inform while letting readers understand the narrator’s changing perspective. Memoir can communicate real processes and personal meaning together.
repair.prompt: An athlete’s memoir reports training changes and describes her disappointment before explaining improvement. Which purpose fits both details?
options: To avoid explaining how learning happened.
To prove all training always succeeds immediately.
To give only fictional entertainment with no real experiences.
To help readers understand the process and her experience of it.
repair.rationale: Memoir can communicate real processes and personal meaning together.

independentCheck.prompt: Which answer uses a detail to explain Goodall’s personality?
options: Watching from a distance rather than forcing closeness supports patience because she allows time for trust.
Watching from a distance showes that she has no need for help.
Watching from a distance proves every animal is harmless.
Watching from a distance proves she never wants to learn about chimps.
independentCheck.rationale: The explanation connects the specific choice to a reasonable, bounded trait.

repair.teach: The explanation connects the specific choice to a reasonable, bounded trait. The choice to wait is evidence of patience without proving an unlimited trait.
repair.prompt: A student postpones checking a birdhouse so a nesting bird will settle. What reasoning best supports “patient”?
options: She accepts waiting rather than forcing an immediate observation.
She abandons the study forever by waiting once.
She must know all future results already.
She must never feel worried in any situation.
repair.rationale: The choice to wait is evidence of patience without proving an unlimited trait.

independentCheck.prompt: What do the examples of David, Goliath, and William in paragraph 48 show?
options: All male chimps have an identical personality.
One observation proves how all animal species behave.
Physical appearance predicts every future action.
Individual chimps differ in their behavior and temperament.
independentCheck.rationale: Contrasting examples support differences among the observed individuals, not a universal claim.

repair.teach: Contrasting examples support differences among the observed individuals, not a universal claim. A conclusion should match the evidence’s scope.
repair.prompt: Two shelter cats respond differently to the same new toy. What conclusion is warranted?
options: These individual animals respond differently in this observation.
All cats everywhere react in one fixed way.
The toy proves appearance determines personality.
No further observations could ever be useful.
repair.rationale: A conclusion should match the evidence’s scope.

independentCheck.prompt: A student says, “It is a memoir because Goodall uses I.” What else should the student explain?
options: Any narrator who uses “I” must be the actual author.
The selection must describe her entire life with no omitted years.
The author recalls real, selected research experiences and reflects on their meaning.
Animal subjects automatically show nonfiction.
independentCheck.rationale: First-person fiction exists, so real remembered experience and reflection are needed.

repair.teach: First-person fiction exists, so real remembered experience and reflection are needed. Distinguish narrative viewpoint from a nonfiction truth claim.
repair.prompt: A first-person story about an invented astronaut uses “I.” Why does that not make it a memoir?
options: First-person narration does not show that the author lived real events.
A memoir must include no personal feelings.
Memoirs never use “I.”
Space subjects can appear only in nonfiction.
repair.rationale: Distinguish narrative viewpoint from a nonfiction truth claim.

independentCheck.prompt: Which sentence has the comma needed between two independent clauses joined by “but”?
options: Although the rain ended, the path remained slippery.
The rain ended but remained heavy in the trees.
The rain ended, leaving the path slippery.
The rain ended, but the path remained slippery.
independentCheck.rationale: The two clauses each have a subject and can stand alone.

repair.teach: The two clauses each have a subject and can stand alone. The repeated subject and complete predicates create two independent clauses.
repair.prompt: Which sentence joins complete thoughts with comma plus “or”?
options: We can rehearse indoors, waiting for the storm.
We can rehearse indoors or outdoors.
If the storm continues, we can rehearse indoors.
We can rehearse indoors, or we can wait for the rain to stop.
repair.rationale: The repeated subject and complete predicates create two independent clauses.

independentCheck.prompt: Where should the comma go in “When the bell rang the visitors entered the hall”?
options: After “visitors.”
After “rang.”
After “entered.”
After “When.”
independentCheck.rationale: “When the bell rang” is the complete introductory dependent clause.

repair.teach: “When the bell rang” is the complete introductory dependent clause. “Because the floor was wet” cannot stand alone as a complete sentence here.
repair.prompt: Where does the introductory dependent clause end in “Because the floor was wet we moved the chairs”?
options: After “moved,” where the comma belongs.
After “Because,” where the comma belongs.
After “wet,” where the comma belongs.
After “we,” where the comma belongs.
repair.rationale: “Because the floor was wet” cannot stand alone as a complete sentence here.

independentCheck.prompt: Using SERIAL-COMMA style, which list is correctly punctuated?
options: The display included maps sketches, and photographs.
The display included, maps, sketches and photographs.
The display included maps, sketches and, photographs.
The display included maps, sketches, and photographs.
independentCheck.rationale: The three parallel items are separated, including the final serial comma.

repair.teach: The three parallel items are separated, including the final serial comma. Each object stays intact and is separated from its neighbors.
repair.prompt: Using SERIAL-COMMA style, select the correctly separated three-item list.
options: The kit held tape, string and, scissors.
The kit held, tape, string and scissors.
The kit held tape, string, and scissors.
The kit held tape string, and scissors.
repair.rationale: Each object stays intact and is separated from its neighbors.

independentCheck.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses a comma after a long opening phrase without adding an extra comma between two actions?
options: During the final hour of the workshop, Sam measured the shelf and cut the wood.
During, the final hour of the workshop Sam measured the shelf and cut the wood.
During the final hour of the workshop Sam measured, the shelf and cut the wood.
During the final hour of the workshop, Sam measured the shelf, and cut the wood.
independentCheck.rationale: The phrase is set off as a unit; “measured” and “cut” share Sam as their subject.

repair.teach: The phrase is set off as a unit; “measured” and “cut” share Sam as their subject. Set off the opening phrase; “practiced” and “memorized” share Dev.
repair.prompt: Choose the correct punctuation for a long opening phrase and two verbs sharing one subject.
options: Throughout the last week of rehearsal, Dev practiced scales and memorized the melody.
Throughout the last week of rehearsal Dev practiced, scales and memorized the melody.
Throughout, the last week of rehearsal Dev practiced scales and memorized the melody.
Throughout the last week of rehearsal, Dev practiced scales, and memorized the melody.
repair.rationale: Set off the opening phrase; “practiced” and “memorized” share Dev.

independentCheck.prompt: Which sentence correctly puts a comma after the opening words “In fact”?
options: In fact the, fabric shrank in warm water.
In, fact the fabric shrank in warm water.
In fact the fabric shrank in warm water.
In fact, the fabric shrank in warm water.
independentCheck.rationale: The comma follows the complete introductory transition “In fact.” The main clause is the fabric shrank in warm water. Check the phrase’s function rather than inserting a comma after its first word.

repair.teach: An introductory transition such as “After all,” “In fact,” or “For example,” is normally set off from the sentence by a comma in the style used here. A transition explains the relationship between ideas. It is not automatically a dependent clause: look for a subject and verb before classifying the sentence.
repair.prompt: Fresh application: use a comma after the introductory transition “For that reason.” Which version places it at that boundary?
options: For that reason Maya measured the sample first.
For, that reason Maya measured the sample first.
For that reason, Maya measured the sample first.
For that reason Maya, measured the sample first.
repair.rationale: Set off the introductory transition as a unit before the main clause. It has no subject–verb pair of its own and is not a dependent clause.

independentCheck.prompt: The trail vanished behind thick vegetation. What does “vanished” mean in this context?
options: disappeared
stayed visible
became louder
moved closer
independentCheck.rationale: “vanished” means disappeared. Explain which action or condition in the sentence supports that meaning.

repair.teach: Use the surrounding action or condition: “vanished” means disappeared. Substitute the meaning and check whether it fits.
repair.prompt: In a new situation, which meaning of “vanished” should stay the same?
options: became louder
disappeared

very unhappy or uncomfortable
well prepared
powerful and confident

unable to move
eager to cooperate
hard to notice

repair.teach: Use the surrounding action or condition: “irritable” means easily annoyed. Substitute the meaning and check whether it fits.
repair.prompt: In a new situation, which meaning of “irritable” should stay the same?
options: eager to cooperate
easily annoyed
unable to move
hard to notice

options: in a way that signals possible harm
in a way that shows approval
without making a sound

options: without making a sound
in a way that signals possible harm
in a way that shows approval
with great accuracy

options: waiting for stronger evidence
acting suddenly without enough thought
making a careful long-term plan
speaking very quietly

imitate another exactly
avoid all contact with
measure the size of
independentCheck.rationale: “dominate” means control or have power over. Explain which action or condition in the sentence supports that meaning.

repair.teach: Use the surrounding action or condition: “dominate” means control or have power over. Substitute the meaning and check whether it fits.
repair.prompt: In a new situation, which meaning of “dominate” should stay the same?
options: avoid all contact with
control or have power over
imitate another exactly
measure the size of

independentCheck.prompt: Which main idea fits both Goodall’s early problems and her later discoveries?
options: Careful work and patience can help people learn important things.
A researcher should stop after the first problem.
One exciting event explains every part of the memoir.
A discovery means that no more research is needed.
independentCheck.rationale: This idea connects her early problems, continued work, and later discoveries. It fits more than one event.

repair.teach: A main idea should connect important events from different parts of the text. It tells a larger point about the topic.
repair.prompt: A true story begins with failed garden experiments and ends with a successful class garden. Which main idea fits the whole story?
options: The first failure decides every later result.
Only the garden’s color matters.
Patience and careful changes can turn problems into progress.
Once a plant grows, no one needs to learn more.
repair.rationale: This idea connects problems, changes, and the later result.

delayed.prompt: Which answer explains Goodall’s purpose using what happens in the memoir?
options: By including a danger scene, she proves her entire purpose is to frighten readers.
By describing a research center, she cancels the importance of early observations.
By showing setbacks, discoveries and growing research, she helps readers understand how knowledge developed.
By naming chimps, she avoids explaining any meaningful ideas.
delayed.rationale: The explanation connects the whole arc to informing readers rather than relying on a single event.

repair.teach: The explanation connects the whole arc to informing readers rather than relying on a single event. Use the arc, not one isolated moment, to explain purpose.
repair.prompt: A memoir follows a beginner from confusion through repeated trials to teaching others. Which purpose explanation uses the whole development?
options: It shows readers how learning grew and why that growth mattered to the writer.
It gives only a list of classroom objects.
It makes the ending unrelated to the beginning.
It proves that the earliest confusion never happened.
repair.rationale: Use the arc, not one isolated moment, to explain purpose.

delayed.prompt: Which statement about Goodall is best supported by the memoir?
options: She completes the research without assistance from anyone.
She succeeds because she never encounters difficulty.
She never needs records because she remembers everything.
She is persistent and observant, while still experiencing fear and depending on support.
delayed.rationale: A defensible claim includes supported strengths without denying fear, records or collaboration.

repair.teach: A defensible claim includes supported strengths without denying fear, records or collaboration. Evidence of fear or help can coexist with persistence and careful work.
repair.prompt: An explorer reports fear during a storm, keeps careful logs and receives help reaching shelter. Which description is defensible?
options: Successful only because no problems occurred.
Never afraid and never helped.
Careless because feeling fear prevents accurate observation.
Careful and persistent, while afraid and supported by others.
repair.rationale: Evidence of fear or help can coexist with persistence and careful work.

delayed.prompt: Why are the observations of older siblings helping with Flint important?
options: They show that chimp families have exactly the same rules as human families.
They give specific evidence of family care and relationships among the chimps.
They show toolmaking is the only subject studied at Gombe.
They prove every chimp in every group always behaves kindly.
delayed.rationale: The observation supports family relationships; broader absolute conclusions are not warranted.

repair.teach: The observation supports family relationships; broader absolute conclusions are not warranted. State the observed social support without adding unsupported absolutes.
repair.prompt: Older otters guide a youngster toward food and remain nearby while it tries. Which conclusion is closest to the evidence?
options: The observation showes that otters use human language.
All otter families behave identically in every situation.
The observed interaction shows support of a youngster’s learning.
The youngster needs no further experience.
repair.rationale: State the observed social support without adding unsupported absolutes.

delayed.prompt: Which comparison correctly distinguishes memoir from a fictional first-person story?
options: A fictional narrator must recount the real author’s entire life.
Memoirs cannot include feelings because nonfiction excludes perspective.
Only memoirs ever use a first-person narrator.
Both may use “I,” but a memoir presents the author’s remembered real experiences and reflection.
delayed.rationale: First person can occur in either genre; the truth claim, personal experience and reflection distinguish memoir.

repair.teach: First person can occur in either genre; the truth claim, personal experience and reflection distinguish memoir. Memoir can focus on selected experiences rather than a full lifespan.
repair.prompt: A writer reflects on a real month caring for an injured horse. What makes this memoir rather than necessarily a whole-life autobiography?
options: Using first person by itself guarantees truth.
The horse must speak invented dialogue.
It must include every event of the author’s entire life.
It selects a meaningful period of the author’s real experience.
repair.rationale: Memoir can focus on selected experiences rather than a full lifespan.

delayed.prompt: Which sentence uses a comma to join two independent clauses with “so”?
options: The microphone failed so unexpectedly during the show.
The microphone failed, so Nia spoke more loudly.
The microphone failed, interrupting the show.
Because the microphone failed, Nia spoke more loudly.
delayed.rationale: Each side of “so” is an independent clause; the other complete examples use different structures.

repair.teach: Each side of “so” is an independent clause; the other complete examples use different structures. Both clauses could stand alone; “for” functions as a coordinating conjunction here.
repair.prompt: Choose the sentence joining two independent clauses with comma plus “for.”
options: We moved the exhibit indoors, avoiding the water.
Because the courtyard was flooding, we moved the exhibit indoors.
We moved the exhibit indoors for protection.
We moved the exhibit indoors, for the courtyard was flooding.
repair.rationale: Both clauses could stand alone; “for” functions as a coordinating conjunction here.

delayed.prompt: Which sentence correctly separates an introductory dependent clause from the main clause?
options: Before, the audience arrived the musicians tuned their instruments.
Before the audience arrived the musicians, tuned their instruments.
Before the audience, arrived the musicians tuned their instruments.
Before the audience arrived, the musicians tuned their instruments.
delayed.rationale: The clause beginning with “Before” ends at “arrived.”

repair.teach: The clause beginning with “Before” ends at “arrived.” The introductory clause ends after “dried.”
repair.prompt: Choose the correct punctuation after the introductory dependent clause.
options: Until the paint dried we left, the sign on the table.
Until the paint dried, we left the sign on the table.
Until the paint, dried we left the sign on the table.
Until, the paint dried we left the sign on the table.
repair.rationale: The introductory clause ends after “dried.”

delayed.prompt: Using SERIAL-COMMA style, which sentence correctly separates three things the team recorded?
options: The team recorded, times, distances and temperatures.
The team recorded times, distances and, temperatures.
The team recorded times distances, and temperatures.
The team recorded times, distances, and temperatures.
delayed.rationale: All three items are separated without breaking an item or the verb from its objects.

repair.teach: All three items are separated without breaking an item or the verb from its objects. The three ingredients are separate series items.
repair.prompt: Using SERIAL-COMMA style, choose the correct sentence.
options: The recipe required flour eggs, and milk.
The recipe required, flour, eggs and milk.
The recipe required flour, eggs and, milk.
The recipe required flour, eggs, and milk.
repair.rationale: The three ingredients are separate series items.

delayed.prompt: Which sentence uses the comma after the long opening phrase without adding an extra comma between two actions?
options: At the far end of the school garden, Ari planted seeds, and watered them.
At the far end of the school garden Ari planted, seeds and watered them.
At the far end, of the school garden Ari planted seeds and watered them.
At the far end of the school garden, Ari planted seeds and watered them.
delayed.rationale: The phrase ends at “garden”; Ari is the single subject of both verbs.

repair.teach: The phrase ends at “garden”; Ari is the single subject of both verbs. The phrase ends after “cabinets”; Mei performs both actions.
repair.prompt: Choose the correct long introductory phrase and shared-subject predicate punctuation.
options: Beyond the row of tall storage cabinets Mei found, the brushes and cleaned them.
Beyond the row of tall storage cabinets, Mei found the brushes, and cleaned them.
Beyond the row of tall storage cabinets, Mei found the brushes and cleaned them.
Beyond the row, of tall storage cabinets Mei found the brushes and cleaned them.
repair.rationale: The phrase ends after “cabinets”; Mei performs both actions.

delayed.prompt: Which sentence correctly puts a comma after the opening words “For example”?
options: For, example a missing label can change a reader’s understanding.
For example, a missing label can change a reader’s understanding.
For example a missing label can change a reader’s understanding.
For example a, missing label can change a reader’s understanding.

repair.teach: An introductory transition such as “After all,” “In fact,” or “For example,” is normally set off from the sentence by a comma in the style used here. A transition explains the relationship between ideas. It is not automatically a dependent clause: look for a subject and verb before classifying the sentence.
repair.prompt: Fresh application: use a comma after the introductory transition “In addition.” Which version places it at that boundary?
options: In addition the diagram needs a scale.
In addition the, diagram needs a scale.
In addition, the diagram needs a scale.
In, addition the diagram needs a scale.
repair.rationale: Set off the introductory transition as a unit before the main clause. It has no subject–verb pair of its own and is not a dependent clause.

studyMap: Goodall’s account traces research from early difficulty to a growing center. Watching patiently, adjusting her approach, preserving observations and receiving help allow her to learn more. David’s termite fishing includes modifying a twig into a tool. The account also describes differences among individuals and family relationships. Goodall reports feelings, dangers and reflections along with discoveries. These real, selected first-person experiences make the selection a memoir. Use this original study map to locate evidence in the complete assigned reader, not as replacement reading.

masteryCheck.prompt: Which statement connects the early observations, the tool discoveries, and the research center at the end?
options: Working alone is the necessary cause of every important research discovery.
Careful observation, persistence, and growing cooperation can produce knowledge that lasts beyond one discovery.
Once a scientist has a successful observation, taking further notes becomes less important.
The most important result is that every chimp behaves in the same predictable way.
masteryCheck.rationale: The beginning, middle, and ending together support a process that produces knowledge. Neither solitary success nor identical behavior fits the whole memoir.

repair.teach: The beginning, middle, and ending together support a process that produces knowledge. Neither solitary success nor identical behavior fits the whole memoir.
repair.prompt: A memoir moves from failed costume trials to revised designs and a workshop where other students learn. Which idea fits the whole account?
options: The first failed trial determines every later result.
A workshop matters only when no one helps its founder.
Revising ideas with evidence and sharing learning can turn setbacks into lasting work.
Only the final costume matters; the process is irrelevant.
repair.rationale: This idea connects difficulty, revision, and a lasting result.

masteryCheck.prompt: Which explanation connects Goodall’s first-person memories with the research information she provides?
options: She informs readers about research through personal experience and reflects on what it revealed.
She uses first person mainly to prove that all remembered events are fictional.
She gives an instruction manual for readers to repeat every action with wild animals.
She entertains through dramatic moments, so the factual observations have no role in her purpose.
masteryCheck.rationale: Personal memories, factual observations, and reflection work together. One exciting scene does not account for the entire selection’s purpose.

repair.teach: Personal memories, factual observations, and reflection work together. One exciting scene does not account for the entire selection’s purpose.
repair.prompt: A writer recalls learning to sew and explains why testing seams changed her designs. Which purpose combines these choices?
options: Only to describe the color of fabric.
To claim design never depends on evidence.
To report every event of her whole life.
To inform through experience and reflect on learning.
repair.rationale: The experiences communicate information and its meaning.

masteryCheck.prompt: Use paragraphs 8–13 and paragraph 61. Choose TWO supported parts of an explanation of Goodall’s success.
options: Her later success proves that she never felt afraid.
She persisted and adjusted how she observed the chimps.
The center makes all her early choices unimportant.
Help and later collaboration also contributed to the work.
masteryCheck.rationale: Her persistent adjustments and the contributions of others are both supported. Success does not prove the absence of fear or make earlier methods irrelevant.

repair.teach: A defensible explanation connects her actions to results while acknowledging help. Success does not justify absolute claims about fearlessness or working alone.
repair.prompt: A student refines a design after setbacks and later teaches it with a club. Which explanation is best supported?
options: Only the final club caused all earlier progress.
The student’s revisions and collaboration both helped the project grow.
Help proves that revision was unnecessary.
One success proves the student never felt uncertain.
repair.rationale: Both individual choices and assistance can contribute to an outcome.

masteryCheck.prompt: Which detail most directly supports making a tool, rather than only using an object?
options: A chimp travels across a familiar valley.
David removes leaves from a twig before using it to get termites.
An observer sees a chimp holding grass.
A chimp eats food that is already within reach.
masteryCheck.rationale: Changing material so it serves a purpose supports toolmaking. Merely holding or using an object does not by itself show change.

repair.teach: Changing material so it serves a purpose supports toolmaking. Merely holding or using an object does not by itself show change.
repair.prompt: Which action shows making a tool?
options: Picking up a ready-made ruler.
Looking at a strip of paper.
Cutting and marking a strip of card to measure a pattern.
Reading a measurement aloud.
repair.rationale: The card is modified into a useful measuring tool.

masteryCheck.prompt: Reread paragraph 56 on PDF page9. Which conclusion stays within the evidence about chimp communication?
options: Calls and gestures communicate information, although the account distinguishes them from words making up a human language.
Gestures that look familiar show that every chimp call is a human word.
Because chimps do not use words as humans do, their calls cannot communicate information.
Only animals that speak a human language can have social relationships.
masteryCheck.rationale: The text supports social communication while explicitly limiting the comparison with human language. Similarity does not show identity.

repair.teach: The text supports social communication while explicitly limiting the comparison with human language. Similarity does not show identity.
repair.prompt: A dog uses different signals when playing and warning. What can this observation support?
options: The dog understands every spoken sentence.
The dog’s signals have no meaning unless they are human words.
Every animal signal has exactly the same meaning.
Signals can convey information without being identical to human language.
repair.rationale: The conclusion recognizes communication without overstating the evidence.

masteryCheck.prompt: Which combination gives the strongest support that this selection is a memoir?
options: Its narrator uses “I,” so the events must be nonfiction.
It has exciting scenes and therefore cannot be nonfiction.
Goodall recalls selected real experiences she participated in and reflects on their meaning.
It mentions dates, so it necessarily tells every event of her entire life.
masteryCheck.rationale: Memoir combines real personal experience, a selected focus, and reflection. First person or dates alone cannot show all those features.

repair.teach: Memoir combines real personal experience, a selected focus, and reflection. First person or dates alone cannot show all those features.
repair.prompt: Which description best fits memoir?

A true account reflecting on one meaningful period of the writer’s life.
A list of dates without personal experience or reflection.
A set of instructions with no remembered experiences.
repair.rationale: Real remembered personal experience plus reflection supports memoir.

repair.rationale: The core meaning is in a way that signals possible harm; a new context changes the situation, not the word’s core meaning here.

teachingSections.title: Reread the memoir
teach: A memoir tells about real events in the writer’s life. Read Goodall’s whole memoir first so you understand what happened.
On your second reading, ask: What problems did she face? What did she learn? How did her work change over time?
When a question names a paragraph, reread that paragraph and the sentences around it. Use a detail from that part to explain your answer.
teachingSections.where: Readings → My Life With the Chimpanzees → PDF pages 1–10 (textbook pp101–110). The memoir has paragraphs 1–61.

example.prompt: How can rereading help you answer a question about Goodall’s work?
example.thinking: I look for the part that answers the question. If the question asks about her early problems, I reread the beginning instead of choosing any detail about a chimp.
example.answer: I would reread paragraphs8–13 to learn about her early problems. The chimps ran away, so she had to change how she watched them.
example.why: The answer tells where to look and explains why that part is useful.

teachingSections.tryPrompt: Where would you reread to learn what her research became?
teachingSections.tryAnswer: Reread paragraphs60–61 on PDF page10. They describe the later research and the center.

teachingSections.title: Find the main idea
teach: The topic is what a text is about. This memoir is about Jane Goodall’s work with chimpanzees. The main idea tells the most important point about that topic.
Goodall keeps trying, watches carefully, gains the chimps’ trust, and makes discoveries. Help from other people also supports her work.
A good main idea fits the whole memoir. Check it against the beginning, middle, and ending. One exciting event is a detail, not the main idea of the whole text.
teachingSections.where: Readings → PDF page2, paragraphs8–10; page3, paragraphs11–17; page6, paragraphs38–39; page10, paragraphs60–61.

example.prompt: What is the main idea of this memoir?
example.thinking: I think about the whole story. I connect her early problems with her later discoveries and the research center.
example.answer: Patient, careful work can lead to important discoveries. At first, the chimps ran away from Goodall. She kept trying and changed her approach. Later, she made discoveries and helped build a research center.
example.why: It gives one main idea and supports it with details from different parts of the memoir.

teachingSections.tryPrompt: Why is “The memoir is about chimps” not a full main idea?
teachingSections.tryAnswer: That names the topic. A main idea must also tell an important point, such as how patient, careful work led to discoveries.

teachingSections.title: Learn the six vocabulary words
teach: Read the sentence around an unfamiliar word. Try a meaning, put it into the sentence, and check whether it makes sense.
Vanished means disappeared. “The deer vanished into the bushes” means the deer could no longer be seen.
Miserable means very unhappy or uncomfortable. “The cold rain made the wait miserable” shows discomfort.
Irritable means easily annoyed. An irritable person may get upset over a small interruption.
Threateningly means in a way that warns of possible harm. A dog that growls threateningly may be warning someone to stay back.
Impetuous means acting quickly without thinking enough. Cutting fabric before measuring it can be an impetuous choice.
Dominate means to control or have power over. Someone who interrupts everyone may try to dominate a discussion.
teachingSections.where: Readings → PDF page2: vanished; page7: miserable, irritable, threateningly; page8: impetuous; page9: dominate. Read the whole sentence around each margin word.

example.prompt: Use “impetuous” in a sentence that shows its meaning.
example.thinking: I need to show a quick choice made without enough thought. The action should help the reader understand the word.
example.answer: I made an impetuous choice when I cut the fabric before checking the pattern, and the sleeve turned out too short.
example.why: The sentence shows both the rushed choice and its result.

teachingSections.tryPrompt: How are irritable and threateningly different?
teachingSections.tryAnswer: Irritable means easily annoyed. Threateningly describes a warning of possible harm. Being annoyed does not always mean threatening someone.

teachingSections.title: Use the comma rules
teach: A subject tells who or what a clause is about. A verb tells an action or a state of being. A clause has a subject and a verb. An independent clause is a complete thought: “Maya kept notes.” A dependent clause needs more to finish its meaning: “Although the camera failed.”
Use a comma before and, but, or so when the word joins two complete thoughts: “The camera failed, but Maya kept notes.” Each side can stand alone.
Do not add a comma just because you see and. “Maya checked the camera and changed the battery” has one subject doing two actions.
Use a comma after a dependent clause at the beginning: “Although the camera failed, Maya kept notes.” The comma goes where the opening clause ends.
Use a comma after a long opening phrase: “After several hours beside the marsh, Maya packed her notebook.” This opening is a phrase because it does not have its own subject and verb.
Use a comma after an opening transition: “For example, Maya recorded the time.” Other examples are “In fact,” and “After all,”.
Use commas in a list of three or more things: “She packed paper, pencils, and binoculars.” In these questions, include the comma before the final and. This is called a serial comma.
teachingSections.where: Use the teacher’s comma rules in the study guide. For sentence examples in the memoir, open Readings and inspect complete sentences; the examples below are original teaching examples.

example.prompt: Why does this sentence need a comma? “Although the clay cracked, I repaired the sculpture.”
example.thinking: I find the two parts. “Although the clay cracked” needs another clause. “I repaired the sculpture” is a complete thought.
example.answer: The comma comes after the opening dependent clause, “Although the clay cracked.” It separates that opening from the complete thought, “I repaired the sculpture.”
example.why: It names both parts and explains why the comma belongs between them.

teachingSections.tryPrompt: Add the comma and explain it: “The costume tore but Maya repaired it.”
teachingSections.tryAnswer: The costume tore, but Maya repaired it. Both sides of but are complete thoughts, so the comma goes before but.

teachingSections.title: Explain the author’s purpose
teach: The author’s purpose is the reason the author wrote the text. Ask: What does Goodall want readers to learn or understand?
Goodall informs readers about her research and what she learned about chimps. She tells about her own experiences and explains why the discoveries mattered.
Her feelings make the memoir interesting, but entertainment is not her only purpose. Her observations also teach readers about chimpanzees.
teachingSections.where: Readings → PDF page6, paragraphs38–39; page10, paragraphs60–61. Compare what happened with the explanation of why it mattered.

example.prompt: Why did Goodall write about the tool discovery?
example.thinking: I explain what the event teaches readers. I do more than name the topic or say that the event was exciting.
example.answer: Goodall wants readers to understand an important discovery about chimps. She describes David changing a twig into a tool and explains why this challenged an old belief about humans.
example.why: It states a purpose and uses a detail to explain that purpose.

teachingSections.tryPrompt: Why is “to entertain readers” only part of Goodall’s purpose?
teachingSections.tryAnswer: The events can be interesting, but Goodall also teaches readers about her research and discoveries.

teachingSections.title: Explain what she learned about chimps
teach: Goodall learned that chimps use tools and can change materials to make tools. David stripped leaves from a twig before using it to get termites.
She learned that chimps are individuals. They have different personalities, and their family relationships affect how they act.
She also saw young chimps learning from others. Chimps use calls and gestures to share information. Some gestures look like human gestures, but their calls are not the same as human language.
When you explain a discovery, tell what she saw and what it helped her understand. Do not make a bigger claim than the detail supports.
teachingSections.where: Readings → PDF page6, paragraphs38–39 (tools); page8, paragraphs48–54 (individuals and family); page9, paragraphs55–56 (learning, calls and gestures).

example.prompt: What did Goodall learn about chimp communication?
example.thinking: I reread paragraph56. Then I explain what the calls and gestures show without claiming that chimps speak just like humans.
example.answer: Goodall learned that chimps share information through calls and gestures. In paragraph56, she describes signals that help chimps know what is happening. Some gestures look like ours, but their calls do not form a language in the same way human words do.
example.why: It explains a discovery, points to a paragraph, and keeps the claim accurate.

teachingSections.tryPrompt: What is the difference between using a tool and making a tool?
teachingSections.tryAnswer: Using a tool means using an object to do a job. Making a tool means changing material so it can do the job, as David did when he removed leaves from a twig.

teachingSections.title: Describe Jane’s personality and success
teach: A personality trait describes how a person usually thinks or acts. Choose a trait, name an action from the text, and explain how the action shows that trait.
Goodall is persistent: she keeps trying after setbacks. She is patient: she gives the chimps time to get used to her. She is careful: she writes down details from her observations.
Her success came from these choices and from help from other people. Success does not mean she was never afraid or that she did everything alone.
teachingSections.where: Readings → PDF pages2–3, paragraphs8–17 (setbacks and adjusted observation); page7, paragraphs45–46 (reflection and records); page10, paragraph61 (collaboration and research center).

example.prompt: How does Goodall’s note-taking show a personality trait?
example.thinking: I choose an action first. Then I explain which trait that action shows.
example.answer: Goodall is careful. In paragraph46, she adds details to her notes while the events are still fresh in her mind. This helps her save useful information for later research.
example.why: It names a trait, gives a detail, and explains how the detail supports the trait.

teachingSections.tryPrompt: How do her early problems help show persistence?
teachingSections.tryAnswer: The chimps kept running away, but Goodall continued trying and changed how she watched them. Keeping at a difficult task shows persistence.

teachingSections.title: Explain why this text is a memoir
teach: A memoir is nonfiction about real experiences from the writer’s own life. The writer looks back and explains what those experiences meant.
Goodall took part in the events she describes. She uses first-person words such as I and my, tells what happened, and shares her thoughts and feelings.
The word I alone does not prove that a text is a memoir. A made-up story can use I, too. A memoir tells real personal experiences and reflects on them.
A memoir usually focuses on a meaningful part of a person’s life. An autobiography usually covers more of the person’s life.
teachingSections.where: Readings → PDF page1, paragraphs1–4 (time, place and participant); page3, paragraph17 (looking back); page10, paragraphs60–61 (later meaning and result).

example.prompt: Why is My Life With the Chimpanzees a memoir?
example.thinking: I check that the events are real, that Goodall took part in them, and that she looks back on what she learned.
example.answer: This text is a memoir because Goodall tells about her own real experiences studying chimps. She describes what she did and how she felt. She also looks back on what she learned and how her research grew.
example.why: It explains several memoir features instead of only pointing to the word I.

teachingSections.tryPrompt: Does every story that uses I count as a memoir? Why or why not?
teachingSections.tryAnswer: No. Fiction can use I. A memoir tells about real experiences from the writer’s life and looks back on what they meant.
